name: Bipi
confidence_why: The only description of Bipi stress is Blust's 2021 sketch, written up from brief 1975 survey elicitation with three teenage speakers, and Blust himself calls stress "generally penultimate" in one breath and "indifferently penultimate or final" with final stress favoured in citation forms in the next, while Sipou and Ray 2004 and Schooling and Schooling 1988 say nothing about stress at all.

catalog_quote: Stress is generally penultimate, with some apparent exceptions. During the beginning stage of elicitation it was recorded as final in [xuwóh] ‘two’, [talóh] ‘three’, [androsíh] ‘nine’, and [saŋón] ‘ten’, but as penultimate in [límέh] ‘five’, and [wónoh] ‘six’. Subsequently, where it was recorded, it was indifferently penultimate or final, with an apparent preference for final stress in citation forms. In words of over three syllables stress placement depends upon the morphological composition of the word. In words with two free morphemes such as [xùwikapέtεw] ‘my ribs’ each morpheme (/xui/, /kapete/) is stressed on the penult. In monomorphemic words exceeding three syllables, which are quite rare, primary stress appears to be penultimate, with secondary stress on alternating syllables to the left, as in [kàlakálo] ‘taro with purple leaves’, or [màlisáwo] ‘my brother-in-law/sister-in-law…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated place (Blust 2021, section 2.2, printed p. 99 = p. 5 of the held offprint). (2) Deciding source: a 2021 grammar sketch by the fieldworker himself, based on brief 1975 survey elicitation; it is nonetheless the only description of Bipi stress in existence. Glottolog has zero grammar/phonology entries for the language, and the two other phonological documents I could locate and downloaded (SIL OPD draft by Sipou & Ray, 3 pp; Schooling & Schooling 1988 survey) say nothing about stress. (3) The classification 'variable' (penultimate as general pattern, but recorded indifferently penult/final with final preferred in citation forms; penult primary + alternating secondaries in long monomorphemes; per-morpheme penult in compounds; no weight) is a faithful reading of Blust's paragraph, including his own hedges.
